messages.content: Write a short story (around 1000 words) about a lighthouse keeper on his last night before the lighthouse gets automated. Quiet, melancholic, no big twist please.

**The Last Watch**

The men from the maritime authority had left at four, after they had shown Arne the grey box that would replace him. It sat bolted to the wall of the lamp room like a fuse cabinet, humming faintly, with a green light that meant everything was well. They had shaken his hand. One of them, the young one with the clipboard, had said that it must feel strange, and Arne had agreed that it did, because that was easier than explaining what it actually felt like.

He made supper the way he always did: two potatoes, a piece of salted cod soaked since morning, butter. He ate at the small table by the window that looked north toward the open water, and he did not turn on the radio. The wind was coming round to the west. He could hear it testing the shutters on the seaward side, the way it had every autumn for thirty-one years, looking for the one that was loose.

At sunset he climbed the stairs. There were one hundred and twelve of them, iron, spiralling around the central column. He had counted them on his first night and never since; his knees kept the number for him now. At the top he opened the hatch into the lamp room and stood for a moment in the strange orange light that came through the glass at that hour, when the sun was low enough to look straight into the lens and the whole great prism caught fire from the wrong side.

The grey box hummed. Its green light was steady.

He did not need to do anything. That was the point of the box. At the right moment a sensor would notice that the sky had darkened past some figure written in a manual, and the lamp would come on, and the lens would begin to turn on its bath of mercury, and the light would go out across the water in its pattern, two long and one short every twenty seconds, exactly as it had when he was the one who made it happen. Ships would see it and know where they were. Nobody aboard them would know the difference.

Arne sat down on the wooden stool by the log desk anyway.

The log was open at today's page. He had written the morning entry in his slow capitals: WIND SW 4, VIS GOOD, SEA MODERATE, ALL IN ORDER. Below that, the last line, empty. The authority wanted the logs returned; they would be kept in an archive in the city, in boxes. He had wondered whether anyone would ever read them. Thirty-one years of wind and visibility. Two drowned men taken off the rocks in the winter of '98. The night the lens jammed and he turned it by hand for six hours, his shoulders burning, counting the seconds aloud so the rhythm would not slip. The birth of his daughter, recorded only as RELIEF KEEPER ON STATION 14:00–08:00, PERSONAL LEAVE, because the log was not the place for that, and because he had not known how to write it.

The light outside thinned to blue. Across the water the village on the mainland was switching itself on, one window at a time, the way it always did, the bakery first.

At 18:47 the box clicked. Something deep in the column gave a soft electrical sigh, and the lamp came on: not with a flare, the way the old paraffin mantle had before the conversion, but all at once, white, complete. The lens began to turn. Its beams swept out over the darkening sea and swept back through the room, across his hands, across the open log, across the grey box with its untroubled green eye.

Two long, one short.

He watched it for an hour. Then, because he had always done it at this hour, he got up and walked the gallery. The wind was strong and cold and full of salt. He went all the way round with one hand on the rail and checked the glass for cracks and the gutters for weed and the horizon for anything that should not be there. There was a fishing boat to the north-east, running home, its own small light rising and falling. He watched it until it was clear of the reef. Nobody had asked him to. Nobody would know.

Back inside, he picked up the pen.

He thought about writing something for the archive, something for whoever might one day open the box in the city and turn to the last page. He thought about writing that the light had never failed on his watch, which was not true, or that he would miss it, which was true but not the right word. He thought about the young man with the clipboard asking whether it felt strange.

In the end he wrote what he had always written.

LAMP LIT 18:47. CHARACTER CORRECT. VESSEL OBSERVED NE, PASSED SAFELY. ALL IN ORDER.

He signed it, and after a moment he added the date, though it was already at the top of the page.

Then he sat with the light going round him until morning, because there was nothing else he would rather have done, and because it seemed wrong, on this night of all nights, to let it keep watch alone.
can you write a shakespearean sonnet about the first bus of the morning? proper rhyme scheme and meter please, my year 10 class is going to pick it apart

**The First Bus**

Before the sun has climbed above the cranes,
the first bus kneels, and sighs, and lets us in:
the nurse whose twelve-hour shift is in her veins,
the baker dusted to the wrist and chin.
We do not speak. The heater ticks and hums;
the windows give us back our tired eyes.
A boy rehearses something with his thumbs;
a woman reads, and smiles at some surprise.
The driver knows us all, but not our names;
he waits a moment for the man who's late,
and through the glass, in pale and passing frames,
the river brightens to a silver plate.
  We are not friends. We'll never be. And yet
  this is the nearest thing to home I get.

---

For the class: the rhyme scheme is ABAB CDCD EFEF GG, in iambic pentameter throughout. The turn (volta) comes at the couplet, where the poem moves from describing the passengers to the speaker's own feeling about them. A detail worth discussing: "the first bus kneels" is literal (low-floor buses lower themselves at the kerb), but the word also carries a hint of devotion. Ask them what that does to the tone of the opening.

I'm writing a fantasy novel and I'm stuck on a scene. Context: Ilsabet is a cartographer at the royal Archive. She notices that the big old map of the southern coast in the archive gallery is slowly redrawing itself, the coastline is moving inland. Nobody else has noticed. Can you write the scene where she sits up overnight and actually sees it happen? Third person past tense, eerie and slow-building, around 800-1000 words. End on an unsettling note but not a cliffhanger.

The map had been wrong for three days before Ilsabet allowed herself to believe it.

On the first morning she blamed the lamp. The great chart of the Southern Reach hung in the east gallery of the Archive, behind glass, under a lamp that the night porter was supposed to trim and seldom did, and in bad light a coastline could seem to shift. She noted the discrepancy in her daybook (*Varrow Point appears foreshortened, cf. survey of 312*) and went back to the boundary dispute she was meant to be settling between two barons, each of whom believed a particular stream belonged to him.

On the second morning she brought her own lamp.

Varrow Point had not been foreshortened. It had been moved. The long finger of land that sheltered the harbour at Ost had drawn back on itself, the way a hand curls when it touches something hot, and the soundings written in the bay beside it had moved with it: tiny numbers in a dead surveyor's hand, fathoms and half-fathoms. They had not been scraped away and rewritten. She bent so close that her breath clouded the glass. The ink was the same ink, faded to the same brown. The numbers were simply somewhere else, as if they had always been there.

She told no one. She told herself it was a copying error, that the chart had been taken down for cleaning and some apprentice had hung a draft in its place. That evening she stayed late and checked the frame. The seal was the Archive's own, the wax unbroken, pressed with the date of the last inspection, four years ago.

On the third morning she came before dawn.

The east gallery was cold and grey, and the map was a darker grey within it, a long rectangle of shadow on the wall. Ilsabet set her lamp on the floor, turned the wick low, and sat down on the bench in front of it with her coat pulled around her, the way she had once sat up with her mother through a fever. She did not know what she was waiting for. She only knew that she would not sleep properly again until she had seen it.

For a long time nothing happened. The Archive settled around her: the tick of cooling stone, the far-off sound of the river under the bridge, a pigeon shifting in the eaves. Her eyes grew heavy. The coastline swam and steadied, swam and steadied.

Then, very quietly, the paper made a sound.

It was not a loud sound. It was the sound a page makes when someone turns it in the next room, a dry, private whisper. Ilsabet was on her feet before she had decided to stand. She raised the lamp.

The ink was moving.

Not quickly. Nothing about it was quick. Along the edge of the Southern Reach, where the coast ran down toward the fishing villages of Mere and Saltholm, a line of brown ink was drawing itself inland a hair's breadth at a time, as if an invisible pen were tracing a new shore with enormous patience. Behind it, where the land had been, the paper was neither scraped nor blank. It was *sea*: the faint stippling the old cartographers used for open water, spreading in the line's wake like frost across a window. The little church symbol that marked Saltholm was still there. It sat in the stippled sea now, a cross inside a circle, alone.

Ilsabet realised she was holding her breath and let it out. The glass fogged, and when it cleared, the line had moved again.

She thought, absurdly, of her first teacher in the Guild, old Master Tennick, who had rapped her knuckles for drawing a river that did not exist. *A map is a promise,* he had told her. *It does not describe the world. It tells the traveller what the world will be when he arrives. Never promise what you cannot keep.*

She had always taken it as a lesson about honesty.

Standing in the cold gallery with the lamp trembling in her hand, she wondered, for the first time and with a slow, sinking dread, whether he had meant it as a warning. Whether the map was not describing the coast at all, but keeping some promise it had made to it. And whether, far to the south, where the fishermen of Saltholm would soon be pushing their boats out into the grey morning, the sea had already begun to keep that promise too.

Behind the glass, very softly, the paper turned another page.

my grandpa Walter died last week, he was 88. I'm his oldest grandchild (26) and I have to speak at the funeral on saturday for about 4 minutes. some things about him: he was a carpenter and built half the furniture in our family's houses, including the big kitchen table at the farmhouse we all grew up eating at. loved fishing on the lake. told terrible jokes, his favourite was "why don't fish play basketball? because they're afraid of the net". married to my grandma Margit for 52 years, she died in 2015. he taught me how to sharpen a chisel when I was a kid. please not too sad, he would have hated that.

I'm sorry about your grandpa. He sounds like a wonderful man. Here's a draft at about four minutes when read at a calm pace. Put your own name in where it says [Name]. I've filled in some details around the chisel story, so change them to what really happened. The true version will always land better.

---

Good morning. For those who don't know me, I'm [Name], Walter's oldest grandchild. As he liked to remind me, that made me the prototype. "The first one's always a bit rough," he'd say. "We got better with practice."

That was Grandpa. If there was a joke to be made, he made it, and if there was a bad joke to be made, he made it twice. Most of you know this one, so say the punchline with me if you like: Why don't fish play basketball? ... Because they're afraid of the net.

He told that joke for at least forty years, and he laughed at it every single time. I've come to think that's a kind of talent: to find the same thing funny for forty years. Most of us can't manage that even with the things we love.

Grandpa was a carpenter, and he was the kind of carpenter who believed things should be built to outlast the people who use them. Look around at the furniture in our family's homes, the shelves and the beds and the cupboards. He built them. And he built the kitchen table at the farmhouse. Every one of us has eaten hundreds of meals at that table. We did our homework on it. We argued at it, made up at it, and played cards at it until two in the morning. He built a table, and then he spent fifty years filling it with people.

When I was a kid, he decided I was old enough to learn how to sharpen a chisel. I thought it would take ten minutes. It took the whole afternoon. Every time I thought I was finished, he'd run his thumb along the edge and say, "Almost." I was furious. When he finally nodded, he took the chisel and shaved a curl off a piece of pine so thin you could read through it. Then he handed it back to me and said, "There. Now you know what 'done' feels like."

I've thought about that sentence more times than I can count: at school, at work, every time I've been tempted to call something finished when it wasn't. He never gave lectures. He just gave you a chisel and waited.

He was married to Grandma Margit for fifty-two years. He used to say she was the only person alive who could out-stubborn him, and he said it as if it were the highest compliment there was. When she died in 2015, something in him got quieter. But he kept going out to the lake. He said the fish didn't care that he was sad, and he found that very restful.

So I'm going to make a guess about where he is now, and I think he'd let me get away with it. He's in a boat, early in the morning, with the mist still on the water. Grandma is sitting in the other seat, telling him he's holding the rod wrong. He's ignoring her. Neither of them has caught a thing. Both of them are perfectly happy.

Grandpa, thank you for the table, for the chisel, for the terrible jokes, and for showing all of us what "done" feels like. You did it beautifully.

We'll take it from here.

---

When you read it aloud, leave a real pause before the punchline of the joke. People will join in, and it gives the whole room a moment to smile together.

- tasting notes: baked apple, cocoa, brown sugar

I'm best man at my best friend's wedding next month and I'm terrible at this. I'm Tom. Groom is Daniel, bride is Priya. Daniel and I have been best friends since we were 11. They met at a pub quiz 4 years ago at the Red Lion, her team beat his on the tie breaker question (capital of Burkina Faso, she knew it, he didn't). On a school camping trip Daniel once LOST a canoe, not capsized, just lost it, still a mystery. Need about 3 minutes, funny but sweet in the end. Nothing about exes please, her grandparents will be there.

Here's a toast that runs about three minutes at a relaxed pace, with pauses for laughs.

---

Good evening, everyone. For those who don't know me, I'm Tom, and I've been Daniel's best friend since we were eleven years old. That means I've had twenty-three years to collect material for tonight and about three minutes to use it. Priya's family, please rest assured: I have been heavily edited.

There are a lot of things I could tell you about Daniel. I could tell you he's loyal and generous. That he's the person you call at two in the morning when your car breaks down on the motorway, and he'll come, and he'll bring a flask of tea, and he will never mention it again until your wedding.

I could also tell you about the school camping trip where Daniel lost a canoe. Not capsized. *Lost.* An entire canoe. He came back to the campsite holding one paddle and said, "It's fine, it's handled." It was not handled. The school sent a letter home. To this day, nobody knows where that canoe went, and I'd like to take this moment, in front of all of you, to give him one last chance to explain.

*(pause, look at Daniel)*

No? Okay.

But the most important thing I can tell you about Daniel happened at the Red Lion pub quiz, four years ago.

Our team had won that quiz three weeks in a row, and we were, if I'm honest, unbearable about it. Then one Tuesday a new team turned up, led by a woman who answered every question with terrifying calm. It came down to the tie-breaker: "What is the capital of Burkina Faso?"

We all looked at Daniel. Daniel looked at the ceiling. Across the room, Priya wrote down "Ouagadougou", spelled it correctly, and handed it in, while Daniel was still saying, "Is it... Burkina City?"

We lost. Daniel was quiet the whole way home. And then, just as we got to his door, he turned to me and said, "I'm going to marry her."

I said, "Mate. You lost one quiz."

He said, "No. I'm going to marry her."

He went back the next Tuesday. And the Tuesday after that. He studied African capitals. He learned to spell Ouagadougou. And eventually he worked up the courage to ask her out, and she said yes, and she has been beating him at quizzes ever since.

Priya, you've made my best friend happier than I have ever seen him. You've made him calmer, and kinder, and you got him to buy proper shoes, which the rest of us failed to do for twenty years. Thank you. And welcome to the family, including the part of it that turns up uninvited for Sunday lunch.

So, if you could all raise your glasses.

To Daniel and Priya. May every question life asks you be one you can answer together, and when it isn't, may Priya be the one holding the pen.

To Daniel and Priya!

---

A few delivery tips: print it in a big font, pause after "*Lost.*" and after "Burkina City", and look at Priya, not the paper, for the last paragraph. If the "I'm going to marry her" moment didn't happen quite like that, ask Daniel what he actually said that night. He'll probably remember.
can you write a bedtime story for my daughter Mila? she's 5 and obsessed with hedgehogs. about 5 minutes to read aloud. gentle, nothing scary, happy sleepy ending

**Pip and the Jar of Moonlight**

At the bottom of a garden, under a hedge that smelled of rain and blackberries, there lived a small hedgehog called Pip.

Pip was a very good hedgehog. He snuffled up beetles. He said good evening to the snails. He curled into a ball when the cat came by, and uncurled again when the cat had gone, and he never once complained about it.

But Pip had one problem. He was afraid of the dark.

This is a tricky thing for a hedgehog, because hedgehogs do almost everything at night. While the children in the big house were tucked up in bed, Pip was supposed to be out exploring: across the lawn, under the fence, all the way to the pond. But the dark beyond the hedge was so big and so black that Pip's little legs went wobbly just looking at it.

"I need a light," Pip decided. "Just a small one. Just enough to take with me."

So one night, when the moon was big and round and silver, Pip found an old jam jar that someone had left by the shed. He rolled it out into the middle of the lawn, where the moonlight was brightest, and he took off the lid.

"There," said Pip. "Now I'll catch some."

He waited. The moonlight shone on the grass. It shone on the shed roof. It shone, very softly, into the jar.

Pip popped the lid back on (quick!) and peeked inside.

The jar was empty. Just glass, and a little bit of old jam.

"Oh," said Pip.

"What are you doing?" asked a voice. It was Old Toad, who lived under the flowerpot by the pond and knew a great many things.

"I'm trying to catch the moonlight," said Pip, "so I can take it with me into the dark. But it won't stay in the jar."

Old Toad blinked his golden eyes slowly, the way toads do when they are thinking.

"Moonlight doesn't like jars," he said. "It likes to be free. But I'll tell you a secret." He leaned in close. "You don't need to carry it. It follows you."

Pip did not believe him. But Old Toad said, "Try it. Walk to the gate, and then look behind you."

So Pip took a deep breath, and he walked, wobble, wobble, out from under the hedge and across the lawn. It was dark. It was very dark. But when he got to the gate, he turned around and looked.

And there was the moon, high above the garden. It had come all the way across the lawn with him! It was shining on the grass behind him, silver as a spoon. It was shining on his own little prickles, so that every one of them twinkled like a tiny star.

"Oh!" said Pip. "It came with me!"

"It always does," said Old Toad, who had hopped along behind him. "Even on cloudy nights, when you can't see it, it's up there, waiting for the clouds to move."

That night Pip went further than he had ever been before. He went under the fence. He went past the vegetable patch. He went all the way to the pond, where the moon was floating on the water like a big silver plate. He said good evening to it, and it shone right back at him.

When he came home to his hedge, just as the sky was turning pink, he was tired and happy, and his tummy was full of beetles.

He still had the jam jar. He didn't need it for moonlight anymore, so he used it to keep his favourite things in: a shiny pebble, a blue feather, and one very small snail shell (empty, he checked).

And Pip the hedgehog curled up in his nest under the hedge, with his nose tucked in and his prickles all soft and sleepy. He slept the whole day through, while the moon waited patiently for him on the other side of the sky.

The end.

---

When you read "wobble, wobble", you can walk your fingers across her blanket. Five-year-olds tend to demand that part every night afterwards.
5 limericks about working from home for our team newsletter. clean humor, nothing about specific people

**Five Limericks from the Home Office**

My office is now the spare room,
where I sit in a glow of half-gloom;
I've a desk and a plant,
and a cat who just can't
stop walking all over my Zoom.

I dressed for the call with great care:
a blazer, a shirt, combed-back hair.
Then I stood for a pen,
and the whole team of ten
saw the shorts and the slippers down there.

"You're on mute!" cried the team to Ms. Pruitt,
who'd just given a speech (and she knew it
was her best of the year),
but the team couldn't hear,
since not one single word had come through it.

At the office the coffee was bad,
but at home it's the best that I've had.
I've a grinder, a scale,
and a gooseneck (all hail!),
and a bank statement, frankly, that's sad.

Now they've called us all back to the floor,
three days every week, maybe more.
So I've packed up my mug
and my plant, and a hug
for the cat, who just yawned at the door.

---

Ms. Pruitt is made up. If anyone on the team happens to have that name, swap in "Ms. Hewitt" (it rhymes with "knew it" and "through it" too).

I'm writing a short play for our community theatre and need one scene. Two estranged sisters, Ruth (50s, stayed in the small town and looked after their mother) and Hanna (40s, moved to the city years ago), are clearing out their late mother's house after the funeral. I want it heavy on subtext, not melodramatic, and NO big reconciliation hug at the end. About 5 minutes on stage. Standard script format with stage directions.

**SCENE THREE**

*A kitchen in a small house, late afternoon. Cardboard boxes on every surface, some taped, some open. RUTH, mid-fifties, in an old cardigan, is wrapping plates in newspaper with practised speed. HANNA, mid-forties, in clothes slightly too good for this, stands at an open cupboard holding a gravy boat.*

HANNA: Keep or charity?

RUTH: *(without looking up)* Charity.

HANNA: It was Grandma's.

RUTH: Then keep it.

HANNA: I didn't say I wanted it. I said it was Grandma's.

RUTH: *(stops; looks at her)* Hanna. There are forty boxes. If we go through the history of every object, we'll be here until Easter.

*Beat. HANNA puts the gravy boat in a box marked KEEP – H. RUTH notices and says nothing.*

HANNA: You've labelled them.

RUTH: Somebody had to.

HANNA: I would have helped.

RUTH: You were in Hamburg.

HANNA: I'm here now.

RUTH: You are. *(She goes back to the plates.)* The cups are above the sink.

*HANNA opens the cupboard above the sink. It is full of mismatched mugs. She takes one down: chipped, with a faded cartoon cat.*

HANNA: She kept this?

RUTH: She drank out of it every morning.

HANNA: I painted this. At school. I was... eight?

RUTH: Nine. Mother's Day. You painted the cat purple because you said cats were boring.

HANNA: *(a small laugh)* They are boring.

RUTH: She used it for thirty-five years. I bought her a proper set once, for her birthday. Bone china. It's still in the box in the hall.

*HANNA turns the mug over in her hands.*

HANNA: You could have told me.

RUTH: Told you what? That she drank coffee?

HANNA: That she... *(She doesn't finish.)*

*RUTH tapes a box shut, loudly.*

RUTH: The bedroom's done. I did it last week. Her clothes went to the church. I kept the blue coat, if you want it.

HANNA: You did the bedroom without me.

RUTH: I did the bedroom, the bathroom, the bank, the pension office, the undertaker, the vicar, the flowers, the notice in the paper and the forty boxes. Yes. Without you.

*Silence.*

HANNA: That's not fair.

RUTH: No. It isn't.

*HANNA sets the mug down on the table very carefully, as if it might break from being looked at. She goes to the dresser and begins to empty a drawer: tea towels, rubber bands, old batteries. At the back, a shoebox. She lifts the lid.*

HANNA: Ruth.

RUTH: Charity.

HANNA: They're letters.

*RUTH stops.*

HANNA: *(reading an envelope)* They're addressed to me. *(Another.)* All of them. *(She flicks through.)* No stamps. They're not even sealed.

RUTH: *(slowly)* I didn't know about those.

HANNA: *(opens one and reads silently; then aloud, flatly)* "Dear Hanna. The pear tree has come out early this year. Ruth says it's the warm winter. I thought of you, because you always said the blossom smelled like soap." *(She lowers it.)* That's it. That's the whole letter.

RUTH: She said that about the tree every spring.

HANNA: *(opens another)* "Dear Hanna. Mrs. Albers' boy got married. You would not believe the hat." *(She almost laughs. She doesn't.)* Why didn't she send them?

RUTH: I don't know.

HANNA: You were here. You were always here. You must know.

RUTH: *(sharp)* I was here. That didn't mean she told me things.

*Beat. Softer.*

RUTH: She asked about you. Every Sunday, when I came for dinner. "Have you heard from Hanna?" And I'd say no, or I'd say you were busy, and she'd say, "Well. She's busy." Just like that. And then she'd talk about the tree.

*HANNA sits at the table with the shoebox on her knees. RUTH stays standing.*

HANNA: I called her. Her birthday. Christmas.

RUTH: I know.

HANNA: She never said anything. She just said everything was fine.

RUTH: Everything was always fine.

*A long pause. RUTH picks up the purple-cat mug, looks at it, and puts it into the KEEP – H box next to the gravy boat. HANNA watches her do it.*

HANNA: Do you want to read them?

RUTH: *(after a moment)* They're not mine.

*She goes back to the plates. Newspaper. Plate. Newspaper. HANNA opens a third envelope and reads it silently. The light outside begins to fade.*

RUTH: *(not looking up)* The pear tree's out again. Did you see? Coming in.

HANNA: *(not looking up)* I saw.

*Lights down.*

**END OF SCENE**

---

A note for the director: the scene depends on the actors *not* playing the anger on the surface. Ruth's list ("the bedroom, the bathroom, the bank...") is strongest when delivered almost as an inventory, and the real emotional beat is Ruth placing the mug in Hanna's box without comment.
write a free verse poem about learning a new language as an adult after moving to another country. not sad exactly, more about the small victories

**Small Victories in a Second Language**

The first week, I bought bread by pointing.
The woman behind the counter
said a word that might have meant *this one?*
and I said *yes*, the only word I owned,
and carried home a loaf I didn't want
and ate it anyway, slowly,
as if it were a lesson.

For months my mouth was a room
with all the furniture in the wrong place.
I walked into the corners of words.
I said *I am cold* when I meant *I am lonely*,
and nobody corrected me,
which was its own kind of answer.

But listen.

Last Tuesday, at the bus stop,
an old man asked me if this was the number twelve,
and I said *no, the twelve stops across the road,
but it's late today, it's always late on Tuesdays*,
all of it, the whole sentence, out loud,
without building it first in my head
like a ship in a bottle.

He nodded. He crossed the road.
He never knew he had just been
the audience at my small premiere.

Last night I dreamed in it for the first time.
Nothing important:
my mother, a kitchen, a lost spoon.
But she spoke to me in this new language,
and I understood her,
and in the dream that didn't seem strange at all.

I woke and lay very still,
unsure which of my two lives
I was supposed to get out of bed in.

Then I got up, and made coffee,
and said good morning to the empty kitchen
in both.
flash fiction, 500-700 words, sci-fi. A child born on a generation ship asks her grandmother (the last person aboard who was born on Earth) what rain was like. Hopeful, not depressing.

**Weather**

On the ship, weather was a schedule.

Every ninth day the agricultural deck ran its mist cycle, and the air between the bean terraces went soft and white for an hour, and the children were allowed to run through it with their arms out. Teo, who was six and had opinions, said it was like running through a cloud. Her grandmother Ama, who was eighty-one and had been born on Earth, said nothing, and Teo noticed that she said nothing, the way children notice everything adults try to keep folded.

"Was rain like the mist?" Teo asked that night, in the narrow bunk room they shared, with the hull humming its low steady note around them.

Ama considered this for a long time. She was the last person aboard who had seen rain, and she had learned to be careful with it, the way you are careful with the last match in the box.

"No," she said at last. "The mist is polite. It waits its turn. Rain didn't wait for anything."

"What did it do?"

"It came when it wanted. Sometimes you'd see it coming across the fields, a grey wall, moving, with the sun still shining on your side. You could stand there and watch it walk toward you. And then it arrived, and it was loud. On the roof, on the leaves, on the road. Everything at once." She drummed her fingers on the blanket, quick and uneven. "Like that. But a thousand times. A million."

Teo drummed too, trying to make it sound like a million.

"Did it hurt?"

"No. Sometimes it was cold. Sometimes it was warm. In summer the warm kind came, and the whole street smelled of hot stone and wet dust. There's a word for that smell. I've forgotten it." She frowned. That bothered her more than she let show: the words going one by one, like lights in a house at night.

"Did people like it?"

Ama laughed, which she did not do often. "Mostly they complained. They carried things over their heads to keep it off. They cancelled picnics. They stayed inside and watched it through the window and said, *what terrible weather*."

Teo was outraged. "But it was *free*. It just *came*."

"Yes," said Ama. "I suppose that's why."

They lay quietly. Through the wall Teo could hear the recyclers moving water from somewhere to somewhere else, all of it counted, every drop with a number. She tried to imagine water nobody had counted. Water that fell out of the sky because it felt like it.

"When we get there," she said, "to the new planet. Will it have rain?"

Ama had read the survey reports so often that her thumb had worn a pale patch on the screen. A thick atmosphere. Oceans. Clouds in the long-range images, white spirals, turning.

"I think so," she said. "But I won't see it, little one. That's a long way off. Your children, maybe. Or theirs."

Teo thought about this with the full seriousness of a six-year-old making a plan.

"Then I'll tell them," she said. "About the grey wall, and the loud roof, and the warm kind. So they'll know what it is when it comes. So they won't complain."

Ama turned her face toward the wall so that Teo wouldn't see it, and when she could trust her voice again she said, "Petrichor."

"What?"

"The smell. Rain on hot stone. It's called petrichor. I just remembered."

Teo repeated it under her breath, carefully, three times, the way you put something precious into a pocket you know you will need later.

Petrichor. Petrichor. Petrichor.

The hull hummed. The water moved in its pipes. And somewhere very far ahead, clouds were gathering over an ocean no one had named yet, in no hurry at all.

I'm the director of a small vocational college (welding, electrical installation, nursing assistants, carpentry, IT support). Graduation ceremony is Friday, about 180 graduates plus families. I need a 5 minute speech. Please avoid the usual clichés like "the future is yours" or "this is not the end but the beginning". A bit of humour is fine.

Good evening, graduates, families, friends, and everyone who drove someone here tonight and is now wondering how long this will take. About five minutes. I've timed it. I run a vocational college; I believe in specifications.

Graduates, look at your hands for a second. Go on, really look.

Those hands have done things this year that most people in this country could not do if their lives depended on it. And some days, lives *will* depend on it. Somewhere out there is a building that will stay standing because one of you made a weld that holds. There is a family that will flick a light switch without a second thought because one of you wired it correctly, and then checked it, and then checked it again, because your instructor would have known if you hadn't. There is an elderly man in a hospital bed who will feel a little less afraid tonight, because one of you sat with him, took his blood pressure, and told him your name.

Nobody will write an article about that. Nobody will clap. That's the strange thing about the work you've chosen: when you do it perfectly, nobody notices. The roof doesn't leak. The network doesn't go down. The patient sleeps. In your line of work, excellence often looks like nothing happening at all.

So I want to use this one evening, the one evening when people *are* clapping, to tell you that we noticed.

We noticed the students who came to a seven o'clock class straight from a night shift. We noticed the ones who failed their first practical exam, came back, failed again, and came back again. We noticed the parents in this room who studied at kitchen tables after the children were asleep, with a circuit diagram on one side and somebody else's maths homework on the other. And we noticed the carpentry students who stayed late to rebuild the workshop door after... well. We all know what happened to the workshop door. We're not going to talk about it. The door is fine now. It's an excellent door.

People will sometimes talk to you as if you took the second-best path. As if real education happens somewhere else, in a building with older stone and longer words. When they do, I'd like you to remember tonight. You have spent the last year or two learning to do real things in the real world, to a standard that can be measured, under the eyes of people who would not let you cut corners. That is not a lesser education. In some ways, it is the most honest kind there is. A bridge doesn't care about your opinion of it. A wire is either connected properly or it isn't. You have learned to work in a world that answers back, and that will make you better at everything, not just your trade.

Here's my one piece of advice, and then I'll let you get to the part where your families take four hundred photos of you holding a certificate.

Keep learning from the people who are better than you. Every workplace you walk into will have someone, usually older, often grumpy, sometimes both, who knows a trick you've never seen. Find that person. Bring them coffee. Ask the questions you're afraid sound stupid. The best tradespeople I've ever met were the ones who, after thirty years, could still say, "Huh. I didn't know you could do it that way."

And one day, sooner than you think, you'll be that person for someone else. Some nervous nineteen-year-old will be standing beside you on a building site, or on a ward, or in a server room, watching your hands. Be patient with them. Somebody was patient with you.

Graduates: this country doesn't run on speeches. It runs on you. Thank you for choosing work that matters, and for doing it well.

Congratulations. Now go and find your families. They're the ones crying.

---

Two lines will land much better if you make them true. In the wiring paragraph, name a real instructor ("because Mr. Okafor would have known if you hadn't"), and replace the workshop door with whatever this year's shared story is. Every class has one, and the laugh of recognition is worth more than any joke I could write.

this is the first paragraph of my mystery novel. my writing group says it's "overwritten". can you tighten it without changing what happens? and tell me what you changed so I can learn from it

"It was a dark and stormy night in the small coastal town of Port Elwin, and Detective Inspector Margaret 'Maggie' Thornbury, who had been a detective for twenty-two long and difficult years and who had seen many terrible things in her career, stood looking down at the dead body that was lying very still on the cold, wet, sandy beach, and she thought to herself that this was going to be a very complicated case indeed, because the body was wearing a wedding dress, but there was no bride missing in Port Elwin, and in fact nobody in the whole town had gotten married for at least six months, which was very strange and suspicious."

Your group is right, but the good news is that the *content* is strong. A body in a wedding dress with no missing bride is a great hook. It's just buried in the middle of a 110-word sentence. Here's a tightened version with the same events:

> The body lay at the tide line in a wedding dress.
>
> Detective Inspector Maggie Thornbury had spent twenty-two years looking at the dead, and she knew trouble when it came dressed in lace. Rain drove in off the harbour and pressed the veil flat against the sand.
>
> No bride was missing in Port Elwin. Nobody in town had married in six months.

That's about 60 words instead of 110. What changed and why:

1. **The strangest image goes first.** "A body in a wedding dress" is your hook, so the reader should meet it in the first line, not after forty words of setup.
2. **Cut what the reader already knows.** "Dead body that was lying very still": a body on a beach in a crime novel is dead and still. "Cold, wet, sandy beach": "tide line" gives you wet and sandy in two words, and the rain gives you cold.
3. **Show her experience instead of stating it.** "Twenty-two long and difficult years... seen many terrible things" tells us she's experienced. "She knew trouble when it came dressed in lace" shows an experienced detective's dry attitude, and it ties back to the dress.
4. **Let the reader draw the conclusion.** "Very complicated case indeed" and "very strange and suspicious" tell readers how to feel. If the facts are strange, and they are, readers will feel it themselves. The two short sentences at the end do that job, like two knocks on a door.
5. **Replace the stock weather.** "It was a dark and stormy night" is probably the most famous cliché opening in English. One concrete detail (rain pressing the veil flat) gives you the storm *and* a creepy image.
6. **Drop the nickname clutter.** "Margaret 'Maggie' Thornbury" makes the reader stop and process two names. Use the one people will call her, and the full name can come up naturally later.
7. **Remove the "she thought to herself" filter.** We're already in her point of view, so her thoughts don't need to be announced.

A rule of thumb to take back to your draft: if a word is "very", "really", "indeed" or "that", try deleting it and see if the sentence gets worse. Usually it gets better.

write a ballad, old-fashioned rhyming folk song style, about a ferryman who keeps rowing across the river every day even after they build a bridge. should have a turn where he ends up being needed after all

**The Ferryman of Kell**

Old Tobin kept the ferry
where the Kell runs broad and slow,
and he'd carried half the valley
on its business, high and low.

He carried brides to weddings
and he carried lads to war;
he rowed back home the ones who came,
and he waited on the shore.

Then the council men from Harrow
came with papers and a plan:
"There's to be a bridge of iron, Tobin,
fit for cart and horse and man."

They raised it in a summer,
with its arches grey and tall,
and the folk went over dry-shod,
and they paid no toll at all.

But every dawn at six o'clock,
come fog or frost or rain,
old Tobin cast his mooring off
and he rowed across again.

"Why row," the young ones asked him,
"when there's none to row across?"
"The river doesn't know," said he,
"that it's suffered such a loss."

So he rowed the empty water
with his lantern burning low,
through twenty years of winters,
till his beard was white as snow.

Then came the night of the great flood,
when the Kell rose black and wild,
and it tore the iron bridge away
like a toy from a careless child.

And the midwife on the far bank
heard a frightened farmer call:
"It's my wife, it's come too early,
and there's no bridge left at all!"

Then out across the roaring dark
came a lantern, burning low,
and a voice called through the thunder:
"Well, come on then, if you'll go."

He rowed her through the flood that night,
eighty-one and stiff of bone,
and the child was born at daybreak,
and he rowed the midwife home.

They built the bridge again, of course,
of stone this time, and strong,
but they left the ferry where it lay,
and they made of it a song.

And if you cross the Kell at dawn
and you hear an oar-stroke near,
the old folk say, "That's Tobin, still.
He's waiting. Never fear."
short horror story, ~500 words, creepy not gory. premise: someone starts getting voicemails from their own phone number

**Missed Call**

The first voicemail came on a Tuesday at 3:14 in the morning, from my own number.

I listened to it over breakfast. Eleven seconds of breathing and, somewhere behind it, a faint regular ticking I couldn't place. Spoofing, I decided. Scammers do it all the time. I deleted it and forgot about it, until the second one came the next night at the same minute.

This time there was a voice. It was very quiet, as if the speaker had their mouth close to the phone and didn't want to wake someone. It said: "Don't open the bathroom window."

It was my voice.

Not similar. Not a good imitation. Mine, with the little catch I get on the letter *w*, which I've had since I was a child and which nobody has ever managed to copy. I played it four times, standing in the kitchen with the hair rising on my arms, and then I went to the bathroom and looked at the window. It was closed. It is always closed. The latch was painted shut years ago.

I called my phone company. A patient young man explained that there was no record of the calls on their side at all. "As far as we can see," he said, "nobody called you."

The third voicemail came the following night. 3:14. Same breathing, same ticking, closer now, and this time I recognised it: the old clock in my hallway, the one with the loud second hand. Whoever was calling was standing in my hallway.

"It's not the window," my voice whispered. "I got it wrong. It's not the window. Don't open the—"

Then a sound. A soft click, like a latch giving way. The message ended.

I didn't sleep after that. I sat up in bed with the light on and the phone in my hand, watching the numbers on the screen. 3:12. 3:13.

At 3:14 the phone lit up. My own name on the screen, calling me.

I didn't answer. I let it ring out. I'm not stupid.

It went to voicemail. I watched the little icon appear. *One new message.*

I've been sitting here for ten minutes now, looking at it. I haven't played it. I don't need to. Because I can hear it already, not from the phone but from the hallway, very faint, through the bedroom door.

The clock, ticking.

And someone breathing, close against the other side, mouth near the wood, trying very hard not to wake me.

Practising, I think. Getting the words right this time.

I self-publish fantasy. Need a back cover blurb (150-200 words) for book 1, "The Salt Crown". Synopsis: Neve, 19, is a salt harvester in a marsh village and can taste lies (they taste like iron). The queen of the coastal kingdom is dying, and whoever brings back the Salt Crown relic from the drowned city of Ysmere becomes heir. Neve's brother Corin is conscripted into the expedition of a noble, Lady Ashcombe, and Neve sneaks along disguised as a porter. Twist: Ashcombe plans to drown the marsh villages to raise the old city. Slow-burn romance with the expedition's cartographer, Idris. Themes: class, family loyalty, truth. Comps: Leigh Bardugo, Naomi Novik. Atmospheric tone. Don't spoil the twist completely.

Here are two versions: a fuller atmospheric one that fits your word count, and a shorter, punchier one for ads or the online store, where people skim.

**Version A: atmospheric (about 185 words)**

In the salt marshes of Lowmere, lies have a taste.

For Neve, it's iron, sharp on her tongue every time someone bends the truth. It's a gift she has learned to keep quiet, because in a village of harvesters who owe everything to the lords upriver, knowing too much is dangerous.

Then the Queen falls ill. By royal decree, whoever recovers the Salt Crown from the drowned city of Ysmere will be named her heir, and the great houses race to claim it. When Neve's brother Corin is conscripted into Lady Ashcombe's expedition, Neve follows, disguised among the porters, determined to bring him home.

But the deeper they travel into the marsh, the more often Neve tastes iron. In Lady Ashcombe's promises. In the maps of Idris, the expedition's quiet cartographer, who seems to know more than he admits. And in the true purpose of the journey: a plan to raise Ysmere from the water, whatever the cost, and the cost may be every home Neve has ever known.

Some truths can save you. Others will drown everything you love.

**Version B: punchy (about 110 words)**

Neve can taste a lie. It tastes like iron.

She has spent nineteen years keeping that secret in the salt marshes of Lowmere. But when her brother is forced to join a noble's quest for the Salt Crown, the relic that will name the dying Queen's heir, Neve slips into the expedition after him.

Now she's surrounded by liars. A lady with a smile like a blade. A cartographer whose maps don't add up. And a plan, hidden beneath the waters of a drowned city, that could sink every village in the marsh.

To save her brother, Neve will have to trust someone.

Everything she tastes says she shouldn't.

**Taglines for the front cover**

- *In the marsh, every lie has a taste.*
- *Some truths can save you. Others will drown everything you love.*

**Comp line** (put it under the blurb or in the store description, not on the front cover): *For fans of Leigh Bardugo and Naomi Novik.*

Both versions reveal that there *is* a dangerous plan involving the villages, without saying who drowns them or how. That gives readers the stakes, and the twist still has room to land.

Write me a literary short story, around 1800-2000 words. A baker working the night shift finds a teenage girl sleeping in the alley behind the bakery. Realistic, warm but not sentimental, and no "police show up and save the day" ending. Third person. I'd like it to be about work and dignity somehow.

**Proof**

Ferhat came in at eleven, as he had for nineteen years, and the first thing he did was turn on the ovens.

There were three of them, steel decks stacked one above the other, and they took ninety minutes to come up to heat. Everything else in the night was arranged around that fact. While they warmed, he weighed flour from the sacks in the storeroom, set the big mixer going with the rye sour he'd fed at six, and laid out the trays for the rolls in rows so straight that his old master in Gaziantep would have grunted, which was the most anyone had ever got out of that man by way of praise. By midnight the bakery smelled of warm metal and yeast and the small ticking of the ovens expanding. By one he was shaping.

He liked the night. People who didn't work it thought it was lonely, but it wasn't lonely. It was quiet, which was a different thing. The street outside the front window was empty except for the occasional taxi and the fox that came through at two to check the bins. Inside there was the radio on low, the hum of the proofer, and his own hands doing what they had done ten thousand times, so that his mind could go wherever it liked, which tonight was nowhere in particular. That was the best kind of night.

At half past two he carried the cardboard out to the back.

The alley behind the bakery was narrow and smelled of rain and of the bins from the kebab shop two doors down. There was a light over the back door, a bare bulb in a wire cage, and in its circle of yellow, wedged into the corner between the step and the recycling bins, someone was asleep.

He stopped with the flattened boxes under his arm.

It was a girl. Fifteen, maybe sixteen. It was hard to tell with the hood up and her knees drawn into her chest. Grey sweatshirt, jeans dark with damp at the hems, white trainers that had been expensive once. A rucksack for a pillow. She had chosen the spot well, he noticed, the way he noticed things in his trade: the bakery's back wall was the warmest in the alley, because the ovens stood against it. The bricks there stayed warm until morning.

She'd found the warm wall. So she had been here before, or she was clever. Probably both.

Ferhat stood there long enough for the cardboard to grow heavy. He was not a man who liked situations. He liked dough, which did what it was supposed to do if you did what you were supposed to do. He thought about calling someone, and then he thought about who he would call and what they would do, and about the girl's face if she woke up with a uniform standing over her. He set the cardboard down very quietly against the wall and went back inside.

At three he took out the first rye loaves. He set two rolls aside on a sheet of paper, the ones with the split tops that he never put in the window anyway, and after a moment he added a third.

When he opened the back door again, she was awake.

She was sitting up with her back pressed into the corner and the rucksack held in front of her like a shield. Her eyes were enormous and very hard. She looked at him the way a cat looks at a dog, already measuring the distance to the end of the alley.

"I'm going," she said. "I'm going, okay? I wasn't doing anything."

"I know," said Ferhat. He held out the paper with the rolls. "These are wrong. The tops split. I can't sell them."

She didn't move.

He set the paper down on the step, halfway between them, and went back inside, and left the door open a hand's width so the warm air and the smell would go out into the alley. Then he went back to the bench and started on the croissants and didn't look.

When he looked ten minutes later, the paper was empty.

---

She was there the next night, and the next. She came after midnight, later than him, and she was always gone before half past five, when Mrs. Haddad arrived to open the shop. Ferhat never saw her arrive or leave. He only saw the shape in the corner by the warm wall and the rolls disappearing, and once, on the fourth night, the cardboard he'd left out for the recycling arranged into a neat sort of mattress underneath her.

On the fifth night it rained hard, and at two in the morning he opened the back door and said into the dark, "You can't sleep in that."

"I'm fine."

"You're wet. You'll get sick." He heard how he sounded: like his own father, gruff, as though kindness were an inconvenience. He didn't know another way to sound. "There's a stool by the proofer. It's warm. You can sit."

A long silence. Rain on the bin lids like gravel.

"You'll call someone."

"I'm a baker," he said, which was not an answer, but she seemed to take it as one.

She sat on the stool by the proofer with her hood up and her hands around a mug of tea with four sugars in it, and she watched him work. She didn't talk. He didn't ask her name, or where she was from, or why the trainers had been expensive once. He had the feeling those were the questions she was waiting for, braced against, the way she'd been braced against the wall in the alley. So he talked about the dough instead.

"This is the country loaf," he said. "Too wet, you think. Everybody thinks so. But you leave it, and it comes together. You don't fight it." He folded the dough over itself on the floured bench, turned it, folded it again. "You fight it, it gets tight. It tears."

She said nothing. But she watched his hands.

At four he showed her how to shape a roll: the dough cupped under the palm, the small circular push against the bench that tightens the skin. Her first one was a lump. Her second was a smaller lump. Her third was almost round, and she looked at it with an expression he hadn't seen on her face before, something unguarded and fierce, as if she had won an argument with it.

"Not bad," he said. It was more than his master had ever said to him.

She shaped eleven more before half past five. He baked them with the others. In the morning, in the window, nobody could tell which ones were hers.

---

Her name was Dani. She told him in the second week, without being asked, while she was weighing salt. Over the following nights she told him other things in pieces, never looking at him: a stepfather, a flat in another city, a mother who believed the stepfather. A friend's sofa that had stopped being available. Some things she didn't tell him, and he could hear the shape of them in the gaps, and he didn't ask about those either.

He thought a great deal in those weeks about what he was supposed to do. He was not a fool. He knew there were rules about children and strangers and back rooms at night, and that he was on the wrong side of most of them. He knew that the warm wall would not last, that winter was coming, that Mrs. Haddad would find out, that one night Dani would simply not be there and he would never know why. He knew that rolls and tea were not a solution to anything.

On the last Sunday of the month, when the bakery was closed, he took the bus across town to the community centre where his sister volunteered and sat with her in the little office for two hours. He came away with a phone number and the name of a woman called Ruth, who ran a place for young people. Not a police place, his sister said. A place with beds and a kitchen, where nobody would send Dani anywhere she didn't want to go. A place that needed, as it turned out, someone to teach the kids in the kitchen on Saturday mornings. They had flour. They didn't have anyone who knew what to do with it.

He didn't know how to say any of this. He practised on the bus home, and everything he tried came out sounding like a lecture or a trap.

In the end, at three on Monday morning, with the first rye out and the croissants proofing, he simply laid the piece of paper with Ruth's number on the bench beside Dani's scale, where she would see it, and went on folding the dough.

She saw it. She read it. She didn't say anything for a long time.

"It's a place with a kitchen," Ferhat told the dough. "They need someone to show them how to shape rolls. On Saturdays. I said I'd come. I'll need an assistant. Someone who knows what she's doing."

"I don't know what I'm doing."

"You know more than they do." He turned the dough. "You don't fight it. It comes together."

She picked up the paper and folded it in half, and in half again, very small, and put it in the pocket of her sweatshirt. She didn't promise anything. He didn't ask her to.

At half past five, when she pulled up her hood and slipped out the back door, the rolls she had shaped were cooling on the rack in straight rows, evenly spaced, their tops tight and unbroken. He looked at them for a while.

Then he put them in the window at the front, where people would see them first.
I need a comic monologue for an audition, about 2 minutes, one character. Ideally a substitute teacher. Clean humour, it's for a family theatre.

**The Hamster Situation**

*MR. PEMBERTON, a substitute teacher in his forties, holds a clipboard like a shield.*

Good morning, Year Five. My name is Mr. Pemberton, and I will be your substitute today, because Mrs. Albright is... *(checks clipboard)* "unwell." I don't know what that means. Nobody told me. I'm choosing to believe it's a cold, and not, for example, you.

*(Beat.)*

Now. Before we begin today's lesson, which is *(checks)* "fractions, gently," the office has asked me to "address something." They didn't say what. But I've been in this room for four minutes, and I have a guess.

Where is the hamster?

*(He looks around the room.)*

There is a cage. On the cage there is a sign that says "MR. NIBBLES. DO NOT FEED HIM CRAYONS." There are, in fact, several crayons in the cage. There is no Mr. Nibbles.

*(He raises a hand.)*

Nobody panic. I'm not panicking. This is my calm voice. I have eleven years of substitute teaching behind me. I have seen a child glue himself to a globe. I was present for the Great Volcano Project, and I still can't smell vinegar without needing to sit down. I can handle a missing hamster.

Here's what's going to happen. I'm going to close my eyes and count to ten. When I open them, Mr. Nibbles will be back in his cage, and we will never speak of this again. No names. No questions. No phone calls home. I am offering you a deal no adult has ever offered you before, and I'd like you to appreciate that.

*(He closes his eyes.)*

One. Two. Three. I can hear whispering. That's fine. Four. Five. Someone is opening a desk. Good. Good instinct. Six. Seven. Why is someone laughing? Eight. Nine. Ten.

*(He opens his eyes. Looks at the cage. A long pause.)*

That is a guinea pig.

*(Beat.)*

Whose guinea pig is that? That is a completely different animal. That isn't even the same *size*. Did you think I wouldn't notice? Do you think adults just... *(He stops. Narrows his eyes.)* How many animals are in this classroom right now?

*(He turns slowly toward the back of the room. Something, offstage, clearly answers.)*

Is that a *rabbit*?

*(He sits down heavily on the edge of the desk and looks at the clipboard. Very quietly:)*

"Fractions, gently."

*(He looks up at the class, defeated but dignified.)*

All right. New lesson. If Year Five has one hamster, one guinea pig and one rabbit, and only one of them is supposed to be here, what fraction of this classroom is legal?

*(Beat.)*

Show your working.

---

It runs about two minutes if you let the pauses breathe, and the pauses do most of the work. The two biggest laughs are usually "That is a guinea pig" and the final line, so give both a clean beat of silence beforehand. Don't rush into them.
